chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from 'Uthman ibn 'Isa from Sama'ah from Abu Basir said:

I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) saying: 'A man came to the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) and said: O Messenger of God, I have performed Dhihar with my wife. He said: 'Free a slave.' He said: 'I do not have one.' He said: 'Then fast two consecutive months.' He said: 'I cannot.' He said: 'Then feed sixty poor people.' He said: 'I do not have.' He said: 'Then the Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) said: I will give charity on your behalf.' So he gave him the cost of feeding sixty poor people and said: 'Go and give this in charity.' He said: 'By the One who sent you with the truth, what is between her two labia is more in need than I and my family.' He said: 'Go and eat and feed your family.'

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: These three narrations are consistent and not contradictory, because the first narration which said: 'If he is unable to perform the expiation, forgiveness does not suffice for it, and it only suffices for what is other than Dhihar, and it is forbidden for him to have intercourse with her,' does not contradict the final narration in which the Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) said to him: 'Eat and feed your family,' after he had given charity on his behalf, for two reasons: one is that it is permissible that when the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) gave charity on his behalf, the expiation fell from him, then he (peace be upon him) treated him in the manner of the weak among people by saying to him: 'Eat, you and your family,' because he saw their need for that. And the second is that he may have permitted this for him on the condition that whenever he is able to perform the expiation, he will give it, according to what the second narration contained which was narrated by Ishaq ibn 'Ammar, and there is no contradiction between them in any case.
ai.seo_question: What is the hierarchy of expiation for Dhihar in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith establishes the hierarchical expiation for Dhihar, culminating in the Prophet’s gift of funds to a man who claimed poverty, instructing him to feed his own family. Shaykh al-Tusi highlights the scholarly resolution of apparent contradictions in narrations, clarifying that the Prophet’s instruction to 'eat and feed your family' either signifies immediate discharge of the obligation or a conditional exemption pending future ability, thereby harmonizing the legal rulings.
